concept.name: Double bottom
concept.definition: A classical bullish reversal pattern in which price in an established downtrend forms two troughs at roughly the same level separated by a moderate rebound, and the pattern completes only when price breaks above the intervening reaction high (resistance). It is read as two successful defenses of the same demand zone. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Sellers push price down to the same low twice and cannot force it lower; when the subsequent rally clears the peak between the two lows, buyers have taken control.
concept.mechanics: Require a prior downtrend of months, two troughs within roughly 3% of each other separated by at least about four weeks, and an intervening advance of roughly 10–20%. Confirmation is a decisive close above the intervening reaction high with expanding volume; broken resistance often becomes support on a retest. The conventional target adds the trough-to-peak height to the resistance break.
concept.formula: Price target = R + (R - T), where T = trough price and R = resistance (intervening reaction high) at the breakout.
concept.failure_modes: Fails when resistance at the intervening peak holds and the downtrend resumes to new lows, or when the breakout occurs on weak volume and quickly collapses back into the range. Bottoms form slowly, so premature entries before confirmation are the dominant error.
concept.misconceptions: That two equal lows alone confirm a bottom — the pattern is void until resistance breaks. Volume matters more than in a double top: a breakout without volume expansion is suspect.
concept.example: A stock falls to $30, rebounds to $37.50, falls back to $30 two months later, then gaps above $37.50 on heavy volume — completing the double bottom with a target near $45.

citations.source: Lo, Mamaysky & Wang, 'Foundations of Technical Analysis' (NBER Working Paper 7613)
